case_study_insert.main_stem: Zenith Power Limited (ZPL) is a private limited company in the renewable energy equipment sector, employing a workforce of 90. Founded in 2012 by Nadia Okafor, it manufactures photovoltaic panels for commercial solar farms and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. ZPL plans to invest $2,400,000 in an automated solar-cell assembly line, financed by a $1,500,000 ten-year bank loan and $900,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $900,000 a year, a variable cost of $84 a unit and a selling price of $120, and currently produces 45,000 units a year, each unit one photovoltaic panel. ZPL faces a quality control problem, with a defect rate of 4.1% on finished panels and rising waste levels in the assembly hall.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The assembly line produced 11,000 panels last quarter with a defect rate of 4.1%, up from 2.6% a year earlier. Customer warranty claims rose from 19 to 37 per month. Average material waste is 6.4% of input. A survey of 400 solar installers found that 72% would pay a 4% premium for panels with a longer warranty, and 55% rank product reliability as their top purchase factor. A training audit shows 24 of 90 assembly workers lack training on the new automated cell handlers; external courses cost $820 per worker.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Zenith Power Limited for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, increasing the cost of ZPL's $1,500,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.0% from $14.00 to $14.70 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale silicon and glass input costs have risen 8.5% year-on-year, while government solar subsidies were cut 6.0% and installation demand grew 7.0%.

questions.question_text: ZPL financed its $2,400,000 automated assembly line with a $1,500,000 bank loan and $900,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for ZPL of using retained profit rather than the bank loan for this investment.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit of $900,000 requires no interest or repayment, so it protects ZPL's cash flow while the company already services a $1,500,000 bank loan and carries fixed costs of $900,000 a year. The interest saved can fund the $820 training courses for 24 workers, improving the quality control problem without raising the $120 selling price or cutting the $36 contribution on each panel.

Point 2: Using internal funds keeps decision-making with founder Nadia Okafor and avoids the security conditions attached to the $1,500,000 loan, so the $2,400,000 assembly line is not at risk of repossession if solar subsidies are cut. It also allows ZPL to act quickly on the 4.1% defect rate and rising waste, since no lender approval is needed to spend the $900,000 on rectifying the automated cell handlers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to ZPL, its financing mix and its investment decision.

questions.question_text: ZPL is promoting its photovoltaic panels to commercial solarfarm buyers. Consider trade exhibitions, social media advertising, or partnerships with solar installers. Which should ZPL choose to promote its panels? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade exhibitions: Industry exhibitions would bring ZPL face to face with many commercial solarfarm buyers and engineering specifiers at once, allowing live demonstration of the automated assembly quality. However, stand fees and travel are expensive for a 90-employee firm servicing a $1,500,000 loan, and the 400 surveyed installers may not all attend, so the cost per genuine lead can be high.

Social media advertising: Targeted campaigns can showcase panel reliability and the falling 4.1% defect rate to a wide audience cheaply, with measurable clicks and enquiries. The 55% of surveyed installers who rank reliability first can be reached with technical content. The weakness is that commercial procurement is relationship-driven, so online interest among the 400 installers may not convert into the large orders needed to absorb 45,000 panels a year.

Partnerships with solar installers: Working directly with installers puts ZPL's panels in front of the people who specify products on real projects. Since 72% of 400 surveyed installers would pay a 4% premium for a longer warranty and 55% rank reliability first, installers can communicate those exact benefits and provide feedback on warranty claims, which rose from 19 to 37 a month. This builds steady, targeted demand rather than one-off awareness.

Recommendation: ZPL should choose partnerships with solar installers, supported by selective social media. Installer partnerships directly reach the 400 decision-makers and convert the finding that 72% would pay a 4% premium into sales, while also feeding back quality information to reduce the 4.1% defect rate. Trade exhibitions are rejected as costly and intermittent for a company with a $1,500,000 loan; social media alone is rejected because it generates weak leads in a relationship-driven market.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to ZPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ZPL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in the context of ZPL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why exhibitions and social media alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: ZPL's autocratic leadership coincides with a quality control problem, a 4.1% defect rate and rising waste. Explain two benefits for ZPL of using quality circles and team working to improve quality and motivation.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Quality circles let the 90 assembly workers meet regularly to identify the causes of the 4.1% defect rate and the 6.4% material waste, using the practical knowledge of people closest to the automated cell handlers. Solving problems in teams raises motivation and gives workers ownership of quality, which is more likely to reduce warranty claims that have risen from 19 to 37 a month than instructions from an autocratic manager.

Point 2: Team working breaks down the hierarchy and encourages the 24 workers lacking training to learn from experienced colleagues, spreading skills needed for the new $2,400,000 assembly line. Higher involvement lowers resistance to change and supports the 55% of surveyed installers who rank reliability first, protecting the $36 contribution on each of the 45,000 panels and making better use of the $820 courses.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ZPL's leadership, defect rate and waste problem.

questions.question_text: ZPL must train 24 assembly workers on the new automated cell handlers. Consider on-the-job training or external courses at $820 per worker. Which should ZPL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the actual assembly line teaches the 24 workers ZPL's own procedures and quality standards, costs no course fees, and keeps them productive while they learn, protecting output of 11,000 panels a quarter. It directly targets the 4.1% defect rate and 6.4% waste, since mistakes can be corrected on the real equipment. Its drawbacks are that experienced trainers lose time, bad habits might spread, and there is no formal certificate to show the 55% of installers who rank reliability highly.

External courses at $820 per worker: These deliver structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification for all 24 workers (24 × $820 = $19,680), affordable against the $2,400,000 investment. They remove workers from the line temporarily, cutting capacity, and the generic content may not match ZPL's exact cell-handler settings, so some on-site practice would still be needed.

Decision: ZPL should choose on-the-job training first, followed by short external certification once the line is stable. On-the-job training is chosen because the urgent 4.1% defect rate and 6.4% waste are best fixed on the actual equipment with no loss of the 45,000-panel output target. Full external training alone is rejected because paying $19,680 and taking 24 people off the line at once would disrupt supply to installers, 72% of whom expect a longer warranty; a recognised certificate can be added later without that disruption.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to ZPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of ZPL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of ZPL with a well-justified decision covering cost, quality urgency and output continuity.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ZPL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $900,000 ÷ ($120 − $84) = $900,000 ÷ $36 = 25,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 25,000 panels a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $120 − $84 = $36. Answer: contribution per unit is $36.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ZPL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. ZPL can compare the 25,000-panel break-even with 45,000 panels actually produced, a margin of safety of 20,000 panels, to judge whether the $2,400,000 assembly line is warranted.
2. Contribution of $36 per panel lets managers model price changes: the 4% premium that 72% of installers would accept for a longer warranty would add to revenue, and its effect on the $84 variable cost can be estimated before launch.
3. Fixed costs of $900,000 and $36 contribution set the 25,000-panel minimum needed to cover costs and service the $1,500,000 bank loan.
4. Labour productivity of 45,000 units ÷ 90 staff = 500 panels per worker can be benchmarked to judge whether the 24 trained workers and falling defect rate are improving efficiency and reducing the 6.4% waste.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 25,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $36 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 45,000-panel output; modelling the 4% warranty premium; loan-service volume for the $1,500,000 debt; and productivity benchmarking at 500 panels per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ZPL's profitability using the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has ZPL's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 35.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.5%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 25.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue grew from $4,000,000 to $5,000,000 while cost of sales rose from $2,800,000 to $3,250,000; gross profit therefore increased from $1,200,000 to $1,750,000. Dividing gross profit by revenue gives 30.0% in 2024 and 35.0% in 2025. Operating profit of $400,000 on $4,000,000 and $625,000 on $5,000,000 produces 10.0% and 12.5%. Operating profit against capital employed of $2,000,000 and $2,500,000 gives 20.0% and 25.0%.

Evaluation: Profitability improved strongly. The gross margin rising from 30.0% to 35.0% shows ZPL kept more of each sales dollar after direct costs, helped by the $36 contribution on each panel despite the 4.1% defect rate. The operating margin improving from 10.0% to 12.5% indicates the $900,000 fixed costs were absorbed more effectively as output grew. Returns on the larger capital base rose from 20.0% to 25.0%, so the $2,400,000 investment looks value-adding. However, interest payable rose from $60,000 to $70,000 as the $1,500,000 loan takes effect, and the 8.5% silicon and glass inflation could squeeze the gross margin if it cannot be passed on.

Conclusion: ZPL's financial performance has improved. All three margins rose together and cost of sales grew more slowly than revenue, so the gain is genuine rather than a pure revenue effect. The main risk is rising input costs and interest, so ZPL should protect the improved margins by addressing the 6.4% waste and seeking the 4% premium that installers will pay.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether ZPL's profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ZPL of reducing the 6.4% material waste in its panel production.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Cutting the 6.4% waste lowers the $84 variable cost per panel and protects the $36 contribution, especially as silicon and glass costs rise 8.5%. It also supports the 72% of 400 surveyed installers who would pay a 4% premium for a longer warranty, because more consistent panels mean fewer of the 37 monthly warranty claims, strengthening ZPL's sustainability and reliability reputation.

Disadvantage: Waste reduction may need investment in better quality control equipment or slower production, which could push up the $900,000 fixed costs or reduce output below the 45,000-panel target and the 500-panel-per-worker productivity. With a 4.1% defect rate already present, rushing to cut waste could inadvertently raise defects, and savings may be small relative to the $2,400,000 already committed to the automated line.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ZPL's waste data, costs and survey findings.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 5.0% minimum wage increase and the 8.5% rise in silicon and glass input costs will affect ZPL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If ZPL's $1,500,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the increase is 0.75 percentage points (4.5% − 3.75%), so extra annual interest is 0.75% × $1,500,000 = $11,250 a year. That is meaningful but still small beside fixed costs of $900,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct cost is nil. Higher rates could also cool solar-farm investment, but the 7.0% demand growth suggests the market is currently strong.

Minimum wage increase (5.0%, to $14.70 per hour): With a workforce of 90, assembly roles are largely hourly-paid, so the rise lifts the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an honest annual total cannot be invented; the defensible comparison is productivity of 45,000 panels ÷ 90 staff = 500 panels per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is manageable; if the 4.1% defect rate worsens, the $36 contribution per panel is squeezed.

Silicon and glass input costs (8.5% rise): These feed the $84 variable cost on each of 45,000 panels. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound can be shown: if all $84 were affected, 8.5% × $84 = $7.14 per panel, which at 45,000 panels would be about $321,300 a year — but materials are only part of variable cost, so the real figure is lower and cannot be stated from the insert. With subsidies cut 6.0%, ZPL has limited ability to pass this on, though 72% of installers would accept a 4% premium for a longer warranty.

Conclusion: The 8.5% rise in silicon and glass costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across every panel, far exceeds the $11,250 interest effect, and is harder to offset than wages because subsidies have fallen 6.0%. The interest rise is the smallest and can be hedged by fixing the rate; the wage rise is manageable at 500 panels per worker. Material inflation directly erodes the $84 variable cost behind the $36 contribution, so it matters most.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to ZPL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on ZPL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of ZPL with a well-justified judgment that material-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
